source_refs.note: Topic 12.2.2 with Figure 12.2 and the Did You Know box, printed pages 275-276.

blocks.text: The ammonia molecule is pyramidal because of the lone pair on nitrogen. When the nitrogen atom uses this lone pair to form ammonium, the ion adopts a tetrahedral shape in which all four bonds are of equal length and strength (Figure 12.2). The ammonium ion is formed by an acid-base reaction: the lone pair accepts a proton from an acid. IUPAC also recommends the names azane for ammonia and azanium for ammonium, from azote, a Greek-derived name for nitrogen meaning 'no life', used in naming derivatives such as sodium azide, NaN3.

blocks.alt: Left: ammonia, N with a lone pair of dots above it and three H atoms, one joined by a hashed bond to the left, one by a solid wedge downwards and one by a plain line to the right. Right: ammonium, the same three bonds plus a fourth H on a plain line straight up, and a + charge beside N.
blocks.caption: Figure 12.2: Pyramidal and tetrahedral shapes of ammonia and ammonium (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 12.2).
